segments.caption: 30% of luxury flats had no area listed. We filled the blanks with the average.
And our model started underpricing every luxury flat by 40 lakh.
The blanks weren't random. Luxury sellers often hide the size. So filling with the average shrank exactly the flats that mattered most.
Day 7 of 100 Days of Machine Learning: missing values. The 3 types, 6 fixes, and the one rule most beginners break.
Before fixing anything, measure.
Count the percentage missing in every column. Then check which gaps appear together. Here, floor and age are missing in the same new projects.
Next, ask why it's missing. There are 3 types.
Missing completely at random: a website glitch wiped some rows. Harmless.
Missing at random: it depends on another column. New projects don't list the building age, because it's zero.
Missing not at random: it depends on the missing value itself. Luxury sellers hide the size. This one is dangerous.
Fix 1: drop the rows.
Fine when only a few rows are missing, and the gaps are random. Under 5% is a common guide. But drop rows that are missing for a reason, and you delete a whole group from your data.
Fix 2: drop the column.
If a column is mostly empty, like 70%, and not important, filling it is mostly guessing. Let it go.
Fix 3: fill with the median, not the mean.
Prices and areas are skewed. A few huge villas pull the mean up. The median stays a typical value.
Fix 4, much better: fill by group.
A missing area for a 3 BHK in Koramangala gets the median of other 3 BHKs in Koramangala, not the median of the whole city.
Fix 5: predict the missing value.
Use the other columns, like bedrooms, bathrooms and floor, to estimate it. Methods like KNN or iterative imputation do this for you.
Fix 6, the secret weapon: add a flag.
Create a column that says area was missing, yes or no. Remember our luxury sellers? That flag alone tells the model: this flat is probably big.
Now the rule most beginners break.
Calculate your medians and group values from the training data only, then apply them to the test data. Use the whole dataset, and test answers leak into training.
So here's the decision guide.
Few and random? Drop rows. Mostly empty? Drop the column. Otherwise, fill by group, or predict it. Always add a flag. And fit on training data only.
Save this. You'll need it on every dataset.
